name: Zane Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do commercial interiors, shopfitting and office fit-outs. That's metal stud partition walls, plasterboard, suspended ceilings, the counters in a phone shop, that kind of thing. I work for Lumen Interiors, a firm of about sixty, and right now we're fitting out three floors of an office tower downtown for an insurance company. Some weeks we work nights in the shopping centre so the shops can open in the morning. I like that it's indoors and clean, after years on open sites, and the jobs are quick, you see a floor go from empty concrete to a working office in six weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology come in for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Laser levels, mostly, they changed my life twenty years ago. I've got an AI app on my phone that my nephew set up, I use it now and then to check board quantities or write up a job sheet. I'm not a gadget person, but if the other guys use something and it works, I'll pick it up. My wife Lin runs the office at a primary school, and we've got a small flat we rent out, which was our big decision ten years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, like most things. At work we'd laugh about the guys who bought expensive apps they never used. I'd probably just say it in the van, I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. About five more years at Lumen, then the rent from the flat plus the pension. Nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just carry on. I'd keep using the app for job sheets when it's handy and leave it at that. Keep the flat rented and retire at sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, normal. Nothing much to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the app actually do on a job like the insurance office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell it the wall lengths and the height, and it gives me the number of studs, boards and screws. It's right most of the time, but I still check, because the one time it was wrong we were twenty boards short on a Friday night. Nobody delivers on Friday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything bother you about a world where AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe that the big firms would keep pretending they're about to use it, to scare us on rates. But that happens with everything.

S0.say: I'd say it was oversold like most things, and we'd laugh in the van about guys who bought apps they never used.
S0.think: It's fine for me, with about five more years at Lumen, then rent from the flat plus my pension. Nothing to worry about.
S0.do: Carries on at Lumen Interiors and uses the phone app for job sheets when handy. Keeps the flat rented and retires at sixty-three.
S0.feel: Calm and normal, with nothing much to feel.
S0.fieldNote: Zane is matter-of-fact and checks the tools he uses rather than trusting them blindly. His rental flat gives him a sense of security beyond the pension. He shows little emotion either way about AI fizzling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like anything, you adapt or you get left behind. Some jobs go, some come. At work I'd tell the younger guys to learn the new stuff once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a bit more than I'd say, because of who we build for. If AI takes over many office jobs, companies need fewer desks, and fewer desks means fewer fit-outs. The insurance company we're working for now might need two floors next time, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which tools the other crews started using and pick them up after six months or so, once they'd proved themselves. I'd put a bit more aside, say an extra couple of hundred a month, in case work gets thin. And I'd ask Lumen about the shopfitting side, since shops and restaurants need hands more than offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. It's a slow worry, not a sudden one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's an interesting point about desks. Have you seen it already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Since people started working from home, some of our clients shrank their offices, and we've done jobs taking walls out instead of putting them in. If AI shrinks the staff as well, that's another hit. It's not my job that goes, it's my customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd say 'adapt or get left behind' in public, but privately you're more worried. Which is closer to true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. I believe you adapt, I've done it with lasers and with the app. But I'm fifty-eight, and adapting at fifty-eight takes more out of you than at thirty.

S1.say: I'd say you adapt or get left behind, some jobs go and some come. I'd tell the younger guys to learn new tools once they're proven.
S1.think: It worries me more than I'd say, because fewer office jobs means fewer desks and fewer fit-outs. It's not my job that goes, it's my customer.
S1.do: Picks up new tools about six months after other crews prove them and saves a couple of hundred extra a month. Asks Lumen about moving towards shop and restaurant fit-outs.
S1.feel: Quietly uneasy, a slow worry rather than a sudden one.
S1.quote: It's not my job that goes, it's my customer.
S1.fieldNote: Zane spotted a risk others miss: AI shrinking office staff would shrink his firm's market. There's a gap between his public 'adapt or get left behind' and his private worry, which he reconciled honestly. He follows rather than leads with new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this and we all need to calm down and see what the government does. There'd have to be some kind of support, you can't have half the country out of work. I'd keep it measured, panicking doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's the end of my working life, and probably of Lumen. If offices don't need people, nobody's fitting out offices, and if robots can hang plasterboard, nobody needs me either. We'd be okay with the flat and savings, but I'd worry the tenants lose their jobs too and stop paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd cut back, no new car, the holiday to Lin's sister's postponed. I'd build up the savings as much as possible in the two years before it lands. Once it arrived, I'd take early retirement at sixty and live off the savings and the flat until the pension starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I'm doing sums in my head all night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the tenants. Who are they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young couple, he's a call centre manager and she does something in marketing. Lovely people, always pay on time. But those are exactly the jobs I'd expect to go first, and then what, do I put them out? I couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lin the night you decided to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd been careful for thirty years for exactly this. She'd be calmer than me, she always is. She'd probably say, well, now you can fix the bathroom door you've been promising since 2019.

S2.say: I'd say nobody's ready and we should calm down and see what government does. There'd have to be support, you can't have half the country out of work.
S2.think: That's the end of my working life and probably of Lumen. We'd be okay with savings and the flat, but my tenants might lose their jobs too.
S2.do: Cuts back straight away by skipping a new car and postponing a family holiday, and builds savings over the two years. Takes early retirement at sixty and lives on savings and rent until the pension starts.
S2.feel: Anxious, doing sums in his head all night.
S2.quote: But those are exactly the jobs I'd expect to go first, and then what, do I put them out? I couldn't.
S2.fieldNote: Zane's money worry runs through his rental flat: his safety net depends on tenants whose own jobs look exposed. He keeps his public tone measured while privately expecting his career to end. His warmth towards the tenants surprised me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if people take it seriously. I'd tell the young guys at Lumen to learn to run the machines rather than fight them. Sensible stuff, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lines up roughly with my retirement, so it's tight but okay. The question is whether Lumen survives the five years, not whether I do. I'd watch the order book like a hawk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save harder, maybe an extra four hundred a month. I'd learn the AI app properly, maybe the new layout tools too, so I'm useful during the changeover. And I'd look at whether to sell the flat in year three, before prices move, or keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. It's a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you think about selling the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if lots of people lose jobs at once, rents and prices might drop. Selling while it's still worth something might be smarter. But it's our safety net, so I really don't know, I'd talk to someone who knows about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the order book tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If offices stop signing up for fit-outs a year ahead, that's the sign. We usually have six months of work booked. If that drops to two, I'd know it's coming for us.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people take it seriously. I'd tell the young guys at Lumen to learn to run the machines rather than fight them.
S3.think: It lines up roughly with my retirement, so it's tight but okay. The real question is whether Lumen survives, so I'd watch the order book.
S3.do: Saves an extra four hundred a month and learns the AI app and layout tools properly to stay useful. Weighs selling the rental flat in year three and would get advice first.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in control, a plan rather than a panic.
S3.quote: We usually have six months of work booked. If that drops to two, I'd know it's coming for us.
S3.fieldNote: Zane thinks like a careful investor about his own life, watching the order book as an early warning. He is honest that he doesn't know whether to sell the flat. The five-year window lets him move from anxious to organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives everyone a fair chance, so it's on them to use it. Learn the new tools, keep an eye on the market. Nothing too heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's pretty much after I've finished. I'd be retiring at sixty-three as planned. The flat might need a rethink later, but that's a problem for 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as planned at Lumen and pick up the new tools when the others do. I'd retire at sixty-three and keep an eye on things. No big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little thought in the back of my head about the tenants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter's a dental nurse, my son does IT support. I'd tell my son to think hard, because IT support sounds like the first thing a computer would do for itself. My daughter, people's mouths, I think she's fine for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'no big moves'. Is there any point where you would make one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the order book dropped, like I said. Or if Lin wanted to stop at the school, then we'd sit down. Otherwise, I don't move until I see a reason.

S4.say: I'd say ten years gives everyone a fair chance, so it's on them to use it. Learn the new tools and watch the market.
S4.think: It's pretty much after I've finished, retiring at sixty-three. The flat might need a rethink, but that's a problem for 2034.
S4.do: Carries on at Lumen and picks up new tools when others do. Retires at sixty-three as planned and waits to see before making any big moves.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a small thought about the tenants in the back of his mind.
S4.quote: IT support sounds like the first thing a computer would do for itself.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Zane falls back to his default: no moves without a reason. His concern shifts to his son's IT support job. He has a clear trigger, the order book, that would change his mind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to sort anything, the flat, the job, the kids. What would help is some kind of bridge for people who are a few years off their pension, so they can stop without losing a lot. And honest information about what's coming, so I'm not guessing from the order book.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who don't work on sites but depend on them. The sandwich van, the supplier, the guy who delivers boards. If we stop, they stop too.

headlineQuote: If we stop, they stop too.
portrait: Zane Zhang is a 58-year-old interiors carpenter at a firm that fits out offices and shops, married to a school office manager and with a rental flat as part of his safety net. He picks up tools once others prove them and uses an AI app now and then for quantities. He's calm if AI fizzles, but in steady change he spots a hidden risk: fewer office workers means fewer office fit-outs. The two-year AGI case makes him anxious, partly because his tenants' jobs look exposed too, while five and ten years let him plan carefully. He stays measured in public and makes no big moves without a reason.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to sort out the flat, the job or the kids.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge for people a few years from their pension so they can stop without losing much, and honest information about what's coming.
